newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swissair likely to discuss new planes, plans.
newsitem.headline: Swissair likely to discuss new planes, plans.

text.p: Swissair's financial outlook and plans to buy new aircraft are likely to dominate a news conference on Thursday, which officially has been called to announce a new holding company structure.
Analysts admit the structure is important for transparency and potential spin-offs, but doubt Swissair would organise such a briefing just to announce a move that has long been flagged.

"A new holding structure is a good excuse for Swissair to talk to journalists and analysts about their expectations for 1996 and 1997 and whether the restructuring programme is on track," said Giorgio Cortiana of Union Bank of Switzerland.
Both briefings take place on Thursday afternoon, the day after a meeting by Swissair's board of directors.

Analysts welcome the holding structure plans, which Swissair began putting into place early this year in an effort to transform a confusing array of individual units from airlines to catering and property into clear operational divisions.
Clear divisions and a small holding compnay at the top would increase financial transparency, especialy in flight operations, and make it easier to spin-off units, analysts said on Monday.

The briefings take place against a backdrop of continued pressure on Swissair's slim profit margins from persistent price erosion, increased supply of flights, misfortunes at ally Sabena and problems with charter operations.
Swissair's shares have been on a downward track ever since highs were reached in March and several key banks, such as UBS and Credit Suisse, recently downgraded their forecasts.

Cortiana has slashed his 1996 net profit forecast to a mere five million Swiss francs ($3.8 million) from a previous 165 million, Kunz has cut his forecast to 30 million from 110 million and Susanne Borer of Bank Vontobel has cut her estimate to 36 million.
In 1995 Swissair reported a net loss of 147 million francs mainly due to restructuring charges of 340 million.

Swissair's board is likely to have decided the airline's financing plan beyond 1999 because a decision is expected on which aircraft should replace the ageing fleet of Boeing 747 jumbo aircraft and Airbus A310 aircraft.
Swissair declined on Monday to confirm an unsourced Swiss newspaper report that it had decided on the Airbus A-330-200.
So there are plenty of reasons for Swissair's new, and more open, management team headed by Philippe Bruggisser to meet journalists and the financial community to state its case.
Analysts have also scaled back their earnings forecasts due to an expected drain from Belgian airline Sabena, in which Swissair owns a 49.5 percent stake.
Analysts expect Sabena to record a 1996 loss of between 150 and 160 million francs of which half, or 75-80 million, will be borne by Swissair and directly affect its bottom line.
The Sabena burden could be even higher if Swissair decides to take provisions for another expected loss in 1997 at Sabena.
Vontobel's Borer estimates an extraordinary charge of 65 million in 1996 to cover Sabena's expected 1997 loss.
Losses at Sabena could also make Swissair write down the value of its holding. Originally Swissair invested some 270 million francs in Sabena shares.
UBS's Cortiana expects Swissair to write-down its stake in Sabena by 170 million francs in 1996.

Financial analysts admit they have little expertise in guessing which type of long-haul aircraft Swissair might pick -- Boeing, Airbus or McDonnell Douglas -- but note the decision has financial, alliance and political aspects.
The cost of replacing eight A310s and five Boeing 747s from the year 2000 will be several billions of francs and financing by lease or purchase is likely to weigh heavily.
Swissair's alliances with Sabena and Austrian Airlines (AUA) will also play a role as both partners have picked Airbus' long-haul model, A340.

The decision also has political overtones as Switzerland, not a member of the European Union, is currently in talks with Brussels over access to its liberalised aviation market and Airbus is built by an EU consortium.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340 ($1=1.3105 Swiss Franc)
